items.title: Routing by task is already how a surgery thinks — it just isn't how the software is sold
items.body: The useful transferable idea from the tier list is not the ranking, it is the admission that different jobs want different tools. AT&T is reported to serve forty per cent of employee queries with open models and keep the expensive frontier ones for genuinely hard work, cutting coding costs by fifty-six per cent for a two per cent quality drop. General practice already reasons this way about people: the HCA does the blood pressure, the GP does the undifferentiated chest pain. The problem is that NHS primary care buys AI as single-product subscriptions, not as a stack, so there is no lever to route the cheap high-volume work — transcription, coding, letter drafting, inbox triage — differently from the small amount of work where you want the best available model and would happily pay for it. Worth asking any scribe vendor which model actually sits behind the product, whether it changes without notice, and what the quality-cost trade-off was that they chose on your behalf.

items.title: The Fable data-retention story is the real procurement lesson, not the pricing
items.body: The Financial Times chart was read as enterprises refusing to pay for the best model. NLW's counter is that the model carries a thirty-day data retention policy, and that alone is enough for a large number of organisations to refuse it outright. For a UK practice this is the whole conversation in miniature. Capability is not the binding constraint on what a surgery can adopt; data processing terms, retention periods, sub-processor lists and whether the DPIA survives contact with the ICB are. A tool two tiers down on somebody's ranking but with zero retention and UK hosting is the better clinical tool, because it is the one you are allowed to use on a real patient. When a vendor's demo is impressive, the next question is not how good the model is but where the audio and the transcript go, and for how long.

items.title: If Zitron's right / if NLW's right — the same defensive move either way
items.body: If NLW is right, the open tier keeps improving, routing becomes ordinary IT, and the cost of ambient documentation falls steadily — good news for a service that will never fund premium licences at scale. If Zitron is right, open models are the first stage of cost-cutting before abandonment, and his structural point bites: distillation needs something to distil from, so if frontier training spend collapses the cheap tier stops improving and then stops being maintained. For a Harrow practice the response is identical under both. Do not build a working week that only functions with one named product; make sure the clinical record holds the finished note in a form the practice owns rather than the vendor; and treat any price you are quoted now as an introductory one, because both men agree the current economics are being subsidised from somewhere. Buy on demonstrated workload relief this month, on terms you could exit in ninety days.
